A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PS3, VILA-HD and 4KPro research. Their text, figures, tables and Appendices A–H support comparison; relocated and renumbered content can be matched.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training experiments, resolution-scaling results, ablations, latency measurements and evaluations on the authors’ 4KPro benchmark.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds vision-encoder comparisons, additional benchmark evaluations and comparisons under matched visual-token budgets.

M1.justification: Sections 2–3 retain the PS3 architecture, contrastive and box-supervision objectives, patch selection and VILA-HD procedure. PS3Lang uses the encoder after VILA-HD joint training, which already existed in v1 Appendix C. SigLIP2 initialization and separate evaluation of that checkpoint change experimental configurations without establishing a new underlying algorithm.

E1.justification: v2 substantially expands evaluation coverage with HRBench4K/8K, MME-RealWorld, CharXiV, SEEDBench-2-Plus, BLINK, MME, MMStar and MMVet, alongside Chinese MMBench evaluations (Tables 3–4). The curated PS3 training corpus and 4KPro construction remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Beyond v1’s SigLIP/C-RADIO comparisons, v2 evaluates SigLIP2, PECore, PELang, AIMv2 and InternViT2.5 in Table 3. Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, InternVL2.5 and PLM enter the MLLM comparisons in Tables 2 and 4. The original token-pruning comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: The main state-of-the-art VILA-HD comparisons switch to SigLIP2-initialized PS3. New experiments match downstream training recipes, approximate encoder sizes and resolutions (Table 3), or visual-token budgets (Table 4). Appendix C also revises benchmark-specific patch allocations, including removing the special 6% V* allocation.

E4.justification: Table 3 newly examines LLM alignment through PS3 versus PS3Lang results and analyzes which task families benefit. The existing architecture, patch-selection, scale-allocation and high-resolution SFT-data ablations, along with appendix qualitative examples, are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report benchmark point estimates without repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added evaluations do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial result matrices in Tables 3–4 and replaces the main VILA-HD results with SigLIP2-based variants. In Table 2, 4KPro accuracy changes from 74.2% to 75.8% at 35% selection, but from 72.6% to 71.0% at 18%. These are results for changed model configurations, not isolated same-setting gains. Original scaling and ablation results remain.

T1.justification: The saliency-score formula in Appendix A, minimum recognizable resolution definition and mathematical descriptions of training and selection are retained. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption or substantive derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add explicit headline claims of superiority over modern vision encoders, including SigLIP2 and Perception Encoder, and update the MLLM comparisons to Qwen2.5-VL. The central contributions—efficient 4K pre-training, VILA-HD scaling and 4KPro—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 interprets weaker MME-RealWorld results as reflecting requirements such as counting beyond basic high-resolution recognition. It also argues that LLM alignment mainly improves language-centric capabilities. These interpretations are new; the existing limitations and future directions in Section 9 are retained.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the 4,000,000-pixel cap for Qwen models in Table 2 and specifies the per-scale patch allocation for the previously reported 35% 4KPro setting in Appendix C. Core pre-training hyperparameters, data-curation instructions and project-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and discussion covering newer encoders, MLLMs and benchmarks, and adopts Perception Encoder’s distinction between encoders with and without LLM alignment. The established research positioning and Section 8 related-work discussion remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: Section 6 gains a dedicated encoder-comparison subsection and reorganizes experiment settings and results within individual comparisons. Model names, the abstract and conclusion are revised, while most method, analysis and appendix prose is retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds a substantial encoder-comparison matrix organized by task family and alignment status (Table 3), a dedicated token-matched high-resolution comparison (Table 4), and expands Table 2. Figure 1 updates its comparator and performance graphics. Existing method diagrams, scaling plots and appendix qualitative figures are retained.

improvement.justification: The controlled encoder comparisons and token-matched tests on independent high-resolution benchmarks substantially strengthen validation beyond v1’s narrower encoder comparisons and 4KPro-centered evidence. The added MME-RealWorld failures also clarify applicability limits. Changed initialization prevents treating updated VILA-HD scores as direct gains over v1, but the stronger controls and independent validation provide a substantial overall quality improvement.
